newsitem.title: USA: Layoffs latest wrinkle in Sunbeam saga.
newsitem.headline: Layoffs latest wrinkle in Sunbeam saga.

text.p: The announcement that a flamboyant executive known as "Chainsaw Al" plans to slash half its work force is just the latest wrinkle in the twisted saga of Sunbeam Corp.

In the past eight years the company has gone through bankruptcy, changed its name from Allegheny International Corp. to Sunbeam-Oster Co. Inc. to Sunbeam Corp., and moved its headquarters -- as its management and ownership changed -- from Pittsburgh to Rhode Island to Fort Lauderdale, Fla.

On Tuesday, Sunbeam Chairman Albert Dunlap intensified his image to that of "Nuclear Al," by announcing a plan to cut about 6,000 of Sunbeam's 12,000 workers, close 39 of its 53 plants and other facilities and eliminate 10,000 products, or nearly nine out of 10 of its products.

He also set ambitious goals, including completing the company's restructuring within 45 days and doubling sales to $2 billion by 1999. Sunbeam announced a $300 million charge for the transformation plan.

Dunlap, author of a book called "Mean Business: How I Save Bad Companies and Make Good Companies Great," laid off more than 10,000 employees and sold more than $2 billion in assets at Scott Paper before selling the company to Kimberly-Clark.

Dunlap's record made him a darling of Wall Street. Sunbeam's stock shot up $6 to $18.50 when his hiring was announced, although investors have been more reserved about long-term prospects for his restructuring.

Sunbeam rose 62.5 cents Wednesday to close at $25.875 on the New York Stock Exchange, as Goldman Sachs upgraded its rating to recommend from buy. It had dropped 50 cents after the announcement on Tuesday.

"When you make a deep cut like this, in the short run it can boost profitibility," said William Werther, a professor of management at the University of Miami Business School. "I don't worry about what Sunbeam's income is going to look like this quarter or next year. I would be concerned about putting my retirement savings in a stock like that and the idea of leaving it for 10 years."

Dunlap has been excoriated as the living symbol of a corporate culture in which top managers make questionable decisions but collect fat compensation packages, while workers lose their livelihoods as cost-cutting teams address company problems by slashing jobs.
"I'm not going to say that that's irresponsible corporate behaviour," outgoing Labour Secretary Robert Reich said in a farewell address to Labour Department staffers in Washington.
"It would be inappropriate and presumptuous of me to make that comment. And so I will not say that," he said wryly, drawing a laugh from the assembled staffers.

Experts said Dunlap's planned cuts at Sunbeam likely were the highest-percentage corporate layoffs ever. Other companies have cut far more people at once -- General Motors Corp. cut 74,000 workers in December 1991, but the reduction was about 17 percent of its massive work force.

"These wholesale firings tend to be done more in my view as kneejerk reactions to trying to get more into the bottom line, which of course is a good thing. But there have been a number of cases I think where people have turned out that they've fired too many people," said Richard Cyert, President Emeritus at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, who was a long-term director of Allegheny International.
Sunbeam, which originated in 1897 as Chicago Flexible Shaft, once was the crown jewel of Allegheny International, a Pittsburgh-based conglomerate that bought it in 1981.

But Allegheny, hit with management problems and a slump in its other businesses, filed for bankruptcy in 1988. Japonica Partners, an investment group that had accumulated the company's debt, created Sunbeam-Oster Co. in 1989, focusing on the company's successful electric appliance brands.
The company went public in 1992 and moved its corporate headquarters to Fort Lauderdale, Fla., in 1993.

Management experts said it was difficult to guess what Sunbeam's latest announcement would mean for the company's long-term prospects. "Sometimes it's not a matter of cutting 6,000 jobs," said the University of Miami's Werther.
"Sometimes it's a matter of saving 6,000 jobs."
